concept.name: Clearinghouse
concept.definition: An entity through which futures, derivatives, and securities transactions are cleared and settled and that interposes itself between counterparties, becoming the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer. A clearing organization registered with the CFTC is a Derivatives Clearing Organization (DCO); in securities markets the same function is performed by a central counterparty such as NSCC.
concept.intuition: After a trade, the clearinghouse steps into the middle so that each trader faces the clearinghouse instead of each other — if one side defaults, the clearinghouse absorbs it.
concept.mechanics: Executed trades are submitted to the clearinghouse, which novates them, nets multilateral obligations, collects initial and variation margin, maintains a default fund, and guarantees performance to non-defaulting clearing members.
concept.failure_modes: Clearing concentrates rather than eliminates risk: extreme price moves can exhaust margin and default-fund resources, and procyclical margin increases can amplify market stress; the clearinghouse itself is a systemically critical single point of failure.
concept.misconceptions: A clearinghouse guarantee is not absolute insurance — it rests on margin adequacy and the default waterfall, and members can be assessed when a default exceeds prefunded resources.
concept.example: CME Clearing becomes the counterparty to both sides of every cleared E-mini S&P 500 futures trade; in U.S. equities, NSCC nets members' daily obligations into a single settlement per security.
